resolution.note:
Both refuters killed every blocking finding, so the row stamps PASS:verify-refuted and this REVISE stays as the record. slides §7 line 9: scope: (a) I read check_slides.md §7 at its current wording with `rule.js slides 7`. The ban covers the *"Not X. Not Y. Z."* construction: two negations used as a drumroll that lead into a declarative payoff. Line 9 of reading-the-return.md is built the other way round. The declarative comes first (*The question that drives the read: what would have caught this earlier in the session?*), and two negations follow it, with nothing after them. The judge admits the trailing Z is missing. That missing Z is the drumroll the rule targets, so this is not "the same tic". It is a claim followed by contrasts that fence it off.

The rule's other sub-items don't reach this line either. It is a pair, not a triple, so the anaphora-triples cap does not apply. It also passes the empty-negation test in check_writing.md §19(a). Both negated questions are ones the reader actually starts with (did it work? should I have prompted better?), and the writing judge's instance says so on the same body: "negates two plausible wrong questions a reader would actually reach for — not empty negation".

(c) There is no accept-note in the maintainer block specific to this line. However, the HEAD slides instance already judged this exact line under §7 and gave it PASS: "reversed and truncated: the affirmed clause (the driving question) comes FIRST, nothing follows the two negations, and it is a pair not a triple". The body line is unchanged since then (it dates from commit 55b65355), so the new REVISE comes from the judge stretching the rule, not from any change to the text. cut-sweep.ae101.md also says the two Not-sentences need the driving question on the same line as their antecedent. The story and strategy judges cite the second Not-clause as the thing that rules out a punitive reading, so cutting it would remove part of what the line is for.

(e) The line is inside the region the rule governs (chunk 1), so the scope question is not in dispute. The rule simply does not match the construction.

The proposed fix, "Not whether the task succeeded or the prompt should have been tighter.", is itself a sentence fragment that opens with Not, so it would not produce the one declarative sentence the rule asks for. / harm: The line doesn't have the shape the rule bans. check_slides.md §7 bans "*Not X. Not Y. Z.*", which is a drumroll: two negations build up to a reveal. Line 9 of curriculum/lectures/reading-the-return.md runs the other way, as "Z? Not X. Not Y." The affirmed question comes first, in italics, and the two negations after it only close off the wrong questions. Nothing is held back for a reveal. The judge admits the line is "missing only the trailing declarative," but that trailing declarative is the whole tic. Calling a reversed pair "the same cadence" just restates the rule; it doesn't show harm to anyone in the room.

(a) Harm: the two negated questions are the actual priors a reader brings to reading a returned session. "Did the task succeed" is the obvious reflex. "Should I have spec'd it tighter" is the fix-it reflex that the deck's closing slide, "Diagnose first, fix later", tells students to switch off: "edit the prompt, add a constraint". The writing judge on this same file checked the line against check_writing.md §19(a), empty negation, and passed it: "negates two plausible wrong questions a reader would actually reach for — not empty negation."

(b) The harm claimed ("reads as machine cadence") is the rule repeated back, not a consequence for the room.

(c) The proposed fix, "Not whether the task succeeded or the prompt should have been tighter.", is still a verbless "Not…" fragment, not the "one declarative" the rule asks for. It also blurs the contrast: two named wrong questions become one merged clause, which weakens the setup for the "Diagnose first" closer.

(e) History check: `git log -S` shows the line dates from 55b65355 (2026-08-02). Commit 3182f24c5 (2026-09-13) only removed its bullet marker and made it a paragraph, "same words". The committed slides instance (curriculum/evals/instances/ae101--lecture--reading-the-return.slides.json, rule_index 7) records an earlier slides judge testing this exact line against §7 and passing it: "reversed and truncated: the affirmed clause (the driving question) comes FIRST, nothing follows the two negations, and it is a pair not a triple." The wording hasn't changed since, so this new finding contradicts a verdict already on record for identical text.
